summary: Two central defenders and two wing-backs.
sourceLabel: How We Play 2-2-3-1 alternative formation guide
idea: Two at the back. Wing-backs give width. Three connect us. One leads the line. When the ball changes, our jobs change.
playerFacing: The formation is where we begin. It isn't where we have to stand. Our wing-backs help us attack but must also help protect our goal.

considerations.label: Points to consider when using this alternative formation
strengths: three players able to combine centrally
players experience dual attacking and defending roles
tradeoffs: two centre-backs may face two or three attackers
central midfielders may block wing-back lanes or fail to cover
the recovery demands may be too great for some teams

reviewQuestions: Is 2-2-3-1 a helpful and intelligible starting notation for two centre-backs, two wing-backs, three midfielders and a striker? Would 2-4-1-1 or 2-3-2-1 communicate the actual responsibilities more honestly?
Is it developmentally suitable as a regular 9v9 system for this particular group, or best as an occasional learning variation?
What are realistic defensive recovery responsibilities and distances for the two wing-backs?
In 2v3 central counterattacks, what are the priority delay and cover actions that can be explained safely to children?
Does "Someone protects the middle" clearly identify the protective job without turning 6 into a fixed defensive specialist?
Does "Lose it? Find home" accidentally encourage abandoning immediate pressure? Would "Press or recover" be clearer?
Where are the natural passing triangles with two wide wing-backs and three interior midfielders? Can the 9 stay connected?
Can the system accommodate rotation and realistic substitution without requiring special player profiles?
Are all diagrams and pressing cues appropriate for the target age and league rules, including offside?
If the qualified reviewer is uncomfortable with the system, do not publish it as a recommended option. Rework or replace it.
notDrawn: Further tactical features and set pieces are not included in this issue.

rules.title: Two stay connected
rules.summary: The two defenders recognise pressure and cover as a partnership.
rules.cue: Am I close enough to help?
rules.extra: One may have to challenge while the other is ready to cover.
look: Do 4 and 5 communicate about who meets the ball?
Is either defender leaving too much space behind?
Can one defender help if the other is beaten?

rules.title: Width with cover
rules.tag: Wing-backs go when someone can protect behind.
rules.summary: Width can help our attack, but it changes the space we must defend.
rules.extra: The covering pattern depends on where the ball, defenders and midfielders are.
look: Is the advancing wing-back offering a useful wide option?
Which teammate recognises the space left behind?
Is the distance to recover realistic for this group?

rules.title: Someone protects the middle
rules.tag: Don't leave the route to our goal open.
rules.summary: A player must notice central danger when teammates support near the ball.
rules.cue: Who is stopping the pass through?
rules.extra: This is a shared team decision, not a permanent instruction for 6 to stay back.
rules.seo: Someone protects the middle: 9v9 2-2-3-1 playing principle
look: Do we recognise when the central route is open?
Can 6 connect play while noticing defensive cover?
Are the other midfielders helping rather than crowding the same area?

rules.title: Lose it? Find home
rules.tag: Press if you can, recover if you can't.
rules.summary: After losing the ball, choose the nearest useful defensive job.
rules.cue: Press, protect or recover: which is my job?
rules.extra: Find home doesn't mean blindly running to a fixed position. The wording itself needs coaching review.
rules.seo: Lose it? Find home: 9v9 2-2-3-1 playing principle
look: Can the nearest player delay the opponent with the ball?
Who covers the central route during the transition?
Are the wing-back recovery demands appropriate for our players?

frames.caption: Example: both central defenders step towards the same opponent, potentially exposing space behind.
frames.altSummary: Two defenders 4 and 5 have moved towards an opponent carrying the ball, leaving another opponent free closer to our goal.

frames.caption: Example: one central defender meets the threat while the other provides depth and cover.
frames.altSummary: Central defender 4 approaches the opponent on the ball; defender 5 remains slightly deeper and nearer goal to provide cover while 6 stays available centrally.

frames.caption: Starting picture: wing-back 2 provides a wide option with central defenders behind.
frames.altSummary: Wing-backs 2 and 3 start in wide positions ahead of defenders 4 and 5; midfield 6 remains central with 8 and 11 nearby.

frames.caption: Example: right wing-back 2 advances wide while the team must decide who covers behind.
frames.altSummary: Wing-back 2 moves up the right side, leaving a channel behind; 5 and 8 may need to consider the danger, but the covering pattern is not yet agreed.

frames.caption: Example: after a turnover, the space behind 2 becomes the next defensive decision.
frames.altSummary: An opponent has the ball on our right while our right wing-back 2 is still high; the team must choose which player delays and which protects the channel.

frames.caption: Example: the central midfielder follows the ball towards the right while a central route may be exposed.
frames.altSummary: With play towards our right, midfielder 6 has drifted towards the wing-back and an opponent can threaten space between our midfield and the two central defenders.

frames.caption: Example: 6 notices the central route and maintains a protective position.
frames.altSummary: As the right wing-back remains high, midfielder 6 stays more central with the two defenders behind; this illustrates an option to protect the direct route to goal.

frames.alt: Stage 1. We lose the ball near our right wing-back, 2, who is high up the pitch. The nearest midfielder, 8, moves to delay the opponent on the ball.
frames.caption: We lose it near our right wing-back. The nearest midfielder, 8, delays.
frames.altSummary: Stage 1. We lose the ball near our right wing-back, 2, who is high up the pitch. The nearest midfielder, 8, moves to delay the opponent on the ball.

frames.alt: Stage 2. 8 delays the ball. Both wing-backs, 3 and 2, track back towards defensive lanes. 6 moves goal-side to screen the central lane.
frames.caption: Both wing-backs track towards defensive lanes. 6 screens the middle.
frames.altSummary: Stage 2. 8 delays the ball. Both wing-backs, 3 and 2, track back towards defensive lanes. 6 moves goal-side to screen the central lane.

frames.alt: Stage 3. The two centre-backs, 4 and 5, move across together towards the ball side, staying connected. The wing-backs and 6 hold their recovered positions.
frames.caption: 4 and 5 move together. A back four is only an outcome of real recovery, not an instant switch.
frames.altSummary: Stage 3. The two centre-backs, 4 and 5, move across together towards the ball side, staying connected. The wing-backs and 6 hold their recovered positions.

issue.intro: An alternative way to organise nine players: two central defenders, two wing-backs, three midfielders and a striker. It asks for careful cover and realistic recovery runs.
issue.summary: The 2-2-3-1: an alternative nine-a-side formation using wing-backs, four playing principles and clear player responsibilities.

roles.title: Goalkeeper
roles.head: See danger early
points: Notice where the ball might go if the team loses possession.
Help the two central defenders see and communicate danger.
Find a sensible passing option rather than forcing play into pressure.
roles.cue: What could happen if we lose this pass?

roles.title: Central defenders
roles.head: Protect each other
points: Stay aware of your partner when deciding whether to challenge.
Recognise opponents threatening the space behind the wing-backs.
Help protect the central route when possession changes.
roles.cue: Am I the pressure or the cover?

roles.title: Wing-backs
roles.head: Two jobs, one decision
points: Offer a wide option when the team has appropriate cover.
Recognise who can protect the area left behind when you advance.
When possession changes, decide whether to delay the ball or recover.
roles.cue: If I leave this space, who has it?

roles.title: Central midfielder
roles.head: Our connection and protection
points: Offer a central passing option without crowding teammates.
Recognise when an advancing wing-back leaves space to defend.
Help protect central passes when the team loses the ball.

roles.title: Interior midfielders
roles.head: Make angles, not crowds
points: Offer different supporting angles to keep possession moving.
Notice where support is needed when the wing-backs advance.
Help the team react when possession is lost.
roles.cue: Am I helping the player on the ball or making it crowded?

roles.title: Striker
roles.head: Give us a way forward
points: Make yourself available for a useful pass.
Look for a teammate close enough to combine with instead of becoming isolated.
Recognise when to put pressure on the ball and when teammates need recovery time.
roles.cue: Can I receive, turn, or help someone run?

gives: possible wide support from two wing-backs
three midfielders who may connect passes centrally
one forward offering a higher passing option
opportunities to discuss when players support and recover
